title: Chapter 7: Repeat Until Done: while Loops
video_title: Python Chapter 7: Repeat Until Done, while Loops
summary: Asha's program gave up after one bad answer, and her checkout took one order only. Follow her as she builds an order loop that keeps going until the customer types done: counters, asking again until an answer is valid, running totals and stop values, while True and break, and trace tables. Then watch her add a limit of three tries with an AI assistant at all six stages, catching two AI mistakes with a test, a trace and by counting the questions.

visual.heading: Today's mission: an order that keeps going
visual.note: The user typed: tea, Cake, coffee, tea, done

segments.say: And a real cafe takes items until the customer says: that is all. So here is today's mission. Asha's order loop asks for an item, again and again.
Coffee is not on the menu, so it says sorry, and asks again.
When the customer types done, the loop stops, and the program prints the items and the total.
One loop, any number of items. Let's build it.

scenes.title: Why this matters

visual.heading: Why this matters
visual.label: The big picture
items: A cash machine asks for your PIN again after a wrong try.
A shop's till scans items until the cashier presses Total.
A game keeps running until you quit.

segments.say: Real programs repeat. A cash machine asks for your PIN again. A shop's till scans items until the cashier presses Total. A game runs until you quit.
Each of these is a loop: a block of code that runs again and again, until a condition says stop.

scenes.title: The idea: check, run, go back
scenes.direction: Teach the loop diagram, then the rule that something must change, then the waiter analogy. Then a quiz and a breather.

visual.heading: while: check, run, go back
visual.label: The idea
body: One run of the block is called a **pass**.
visual.pre:
+--------------------------+
        |                          |
        v                          |
   table <= 3 ?                    |
    /        \                     |
 True        False                 |
   |           |                   |
 run the     continue after        |
 block       the loop              |
   |                               |
   +-------------------------------+
     (go back and check again)

segments.say: A while loop checks a condition, the same way as if. If it is True, Python runs the indented block.
But then, unlike if, Python goes back to the top and checks the condition again. One run of the block is called a pass.
When the condition is False, Python skips the block, and continues after the loop.

visual.heading: The one rule of every loop
visual.label: The idea
items: Something inside the block must change the value that the condition checks.
If nothing changes, the condition stays `True`, and the loop never ends.
Like a waiter who asks every table "Anything else?", but never notices when to stop.

segments.say: Here is the one rule of every loop. Something inside the block must change the value that the condition checks.
If nothing changes, the condition stays True forever, and the loop never ends.
Think of a waiter who asks every table: anything else? Unlike a real waiter, Python never gets tired, and never notices that something is wrong.

visual.question: What must a line inside a `while` loop do, so that the loop can end?
options: Change a value the condition checks
visual.explain: Only a change to the checked value can make the condition `False`.

segments.say: Quick check. What must a line inside a while loop do, so that the loop can end?

after.say: C. Change a value that the condition checks. That is the only way the condition can become False.

items: `while` checks, runs the block, and goes back.
One run of the block is a pass.
Something inside must change, or the loop never ends.

segments.say: Take a breather. Here is what you know so far.
Next, Asha serves her first tables, one pass at a time.

scenes.title: Step 1: A counter
scenes.direction: The file types in. Name the counter and the line that changes it, then ask how many tables are served.

segments.say: Step 1. Asha serves tables 1 to 3. Line 2 creates a counter, table, and sets it to 1. A counter is a variable that counts the passes.
Line 3 is the loop: while table is less than or equal to 3.
Line 4 prints the table number. Line 5 adds 1 to the counter. That is the line that changes the value the condition checks.
Line 6 is not indented, so it is outside the loop.

ask.question: How many times does line 4 print, and which line prints last?

after.say: Three times: tables 1, 2 and 3.
After the third pass, table is 4. 4 is not less than or equal to 3, so the loop ends, and line 6 prints once.

scenes.title: Step 2: Ask again until valid
scenes.direction: This fixes the Chapter 6 problem. Teach the two input lines, ask how many messages, reveal.

visual.heading: Step 2: Ask again until the answer is valid
visual.note: The user will type: 0, then -2, then 4

segments.say: Step 2. This fixes the problem from Chapter 6. Line 2 asks once, before the loop, so people has a value when line 3 checks it.
Line 3: while people is less than 1. Line 4 explains the rule.
And line 5 asks again, inside the loop. That new answer is the change that can end the loop.

ask.question: The user types `0`, then `-2`, then `4`. How many times does `Please type 1 or more.` print?

after.say: Twice. Once for 0, and once for minus 2. Both are less than 1.
Then 4 makes the condition False. The loop ends, and line 6 shows the table.

scenes.title: Step 3: A running total
scenes.direction: Teach the running total, the stop value and plus equals. Ask whether the stop value is added, then reveal.

segments.say: Step 3. Asha adds up prices. Line 2 starts a running total at 0: a variable that grows on every pass. Line 3 starts a counter.
Line 4 asks for the first price, before the loop. The user types 0 to finish. A value that means stop is called a stop value. Line 5 loops while the price is not 0.
Line 6 says total plus equals price. That is short for: total equals total plus price. Line 7 adds 1 to the count, the same way. And minus equals takes away, in the same way.
And line 8 asks for the next price, as the last line of the pass.

ask.question: The user types `3.5`, `4`, `2.25`, then `0`. What are the items and the total?

after.say: Three items, and a total of 9.75.
The stop value is not added. Line 5 checks the 0 first, so line 6 never adds it.

scenes.title: Step 4: while True and break
scenes.direction: Teach while True and break, ask what Done does, reveal.

visual.heading: Step 4: Stop from inside with break
visual.note: The user will type: tea, Cake, then Done

segments.say: Step 4. Line 2 says while True. That condition never becomes False on its own.
Line 3 asks for an item, and cleans it with strip and lower, as in Chapter 6.
Lines 4 and 5: if the item is done, break. Break ends the loop immediately, and Python continues after it.

ask.question: The user types `Done` with a capital D. Does line 6 run for that answer?

after.say: No. Strip and lower turn Done into done, so break runs first, and line 6 is skipped.
Then line 7 runs after the loop: order closed.

visual.question: `cups = 1`, then `while cups < 5:` with `cups = cups + 2` inside. What is `cups` after the loop?
visual.explain: 1 becomes 3, then 5. 5 < 5 is False, so the loop ends at 5.

segments.say: Quick check. Cups starts at 1. While cups is less than 5, cups goes up by 2. What is cups after the loop?

after.say: A. 5. 1 becomes 3, then 5. 5 is not less than 5, so the loop ends.

items: Ask before the loop, and again inside it.
`total += price` adds to a running total.
`break` ends a loop immediately.

segments.say: Breather. Sit back, and take a slow breath.
Next, a tool that shows exactly what a loop does: the trace table.

scenes.title: Step 5: A trace table
scenes.direction: Teach the trace table on the doubling loop, row by row, then ask for the last number, then reveal.

visual.heading: Step 5: Trace the loop
visual.hidden_text: Fill in the trace table first.

segments.say: Step 5. Cups starts at 1. While cups is less than 20, line 4 doubles it, and line 5 prints it.
A trace table writes down the value of each variable on every pass. Let's fill one in.
Pass 1. Cups is 1. 1 is less than 20, so it doubles to 2.
Pass 2: 2 becomes 4. Pass 3: 4 becomes 8.
Pass 4: 8 becomes 16.
Now cups is 16 at the check. Fill in the next row in your head.

ask.question: What is the last number that line 5 prints: 16 or 32?

after.say: 32. 16 is still less than 20, so pass 5 runs completely, and doubles it to 32.
Only then does the check find False. Python checks the condition only at the top of each pass.

segments.say: And the real run agrees with the table: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, then stopped at 32.

scenes.title: See the outcome: the order loop
scenes.direction: Return to the mission. Explain every group of lines, ask for the items and total, reveal. Hand over to the AI story.

visual.heading: Mission complete: the order loop
visual.note: The user will type: tea, Cake, coffee, tea, done

segments.say: Back to the mission. Lines 2 and 3 start a running total and a counter at 0.
Line 4 starts the loop with while True. Lines 5 to 7 ask for an item, clean it, and break on done.
Lines 8 to 13 are the decisions from Chapter 6. Tea adds 3.5, cake adds 4, and each adds 1 to the count.
Lines 14 and 15 catch anything else. And lines 16 and 17 run once, after the loop.

ask.question: The user types tea, Cake, coffee, tea, done. What are the items and the total?

after.say: Coffee gets a sorry, and changes nothing.
Two teas and a cake: 3 items, and 3.5 plus 4 plus 3.5 is 11.00.
Mission complete! Next, Asha protects the How many teas question. She uses an AI assistant, one stage at a time.

scenes.title: Work with AI: six stages, one limit
scenes.direction: Teach the tracing skill. Then one conversation per stage, all about the teas question and a limit of 3 tries. Stage 3 plants the mistake, stages 4 and 5 catch it, stage 6 catches a second.

visual.heading: This chapter's AI skill: tracing
visual.label: Before you start
items: Ask AI to trace a loop for one set of answers, one line per pass.
A trace shows which value changes on each pass, and which never does.
Run the same answers yourself. Never paste private data.

segments.say: This chapter's AI skill is tracing. You ask the AI to trace a loop for one set of answers, one line per pass.
Then you run the same answers yourself. And the safety habits from Chapter 1 still apply.

visual.heading: Plan: the condition and the test answers

messages.text: I am a beginner learning while loops. The number of teas must be from 1 to 10. If it is not, my program asks again. Do not write code yet. Tell me the loop condition, which value must change inside the loop, and some test answers.

1. Repeat while teas is less than 1 or more than 10.
2. Inside the loop, ask again and store the new answer in `teas`. That is the value that can end the loop.
3. Test answers: 3. Then 0, then 3. Then 12, then 3. And the boundary values 1 and 10.

segments.say: Stage 1: plan. The number of teas must be from 1 to 10. Asha asks for the loop condition, the value that must change, and test answers. No code yet.
The AI names the condition, says the new answer is what ends the loop, and lists test answers, including 1 and 10, the points where the result changes. These are called boundary values.

visual.heading: Write it yourself, then ask for a trace

messages.text: I wrote the loop myself. Do not change it. Trace it for the answers 0, then 12, then 3: one line per pass.

Pass 1: `teas` is 0. The condition is True: message, then the answer 12.
Pass 2: `teas` is 12. True: message, then the answer 3.
Check: `teas` is 3. False, so the loop ends and line 6 prints `Teas: 3`.
My trace said the same. I ran it:

segments.say: Stage 2: write. Asha writes the loop herself, and asks the AI to trace it for 0, 12 and 3. The AI traces two passes, then a check that is False.
Asha traced it too, and she runs it. All three agree.

visual.heading: Generate: add a limit of 3 tries

messages.text: Add a limit to my loop: at most 3 tries. After 3 wrong answers, print 'Too many tries. Using 1 tea.' and use 1. If the answers are 0, 0 and 0, tell me exactly what it prints.
Here is the code. With 0, 0 and 0 it asks 3 times, then prints `Too many tries. Using 1 tea.` and `Teas: 1`.

segments.say: Stage 3: generate. Asha wants a limit: at most 3 tries, and then use 1 tea. She asks what 0, 0 and 0 print.
The AI says: three questions, then too many tries. It gives no warning at all.
Look at the condition on line 4, and remember the one rule of every loop.

ask.question: Line 4 checks `tries < 3`. Which line inside the loop changes `tries`?

after.say: None of them. Lines 5 and 6 print and ask, but tries stays 1. Asha suspects a bug. Now she proves it with tests.

messages.text: Before I trust it, list the edge cases, with the exact output each one should give.

1. `1`: Teas: 1. 2. `10`: Teas: 10. These are the boundary values.
3. `11`, then `5`: two questions, then Teas: 5.
4. `0`, `0`, then `5`: three questions, then Teas: 5.
5. `0`, `0`, `0`: three questions, then Too many tries. Using 1 tea.
I ran case 4 on your code. It passes:

segments.say: Stage 4: test. Asha asks for edge cases: unusual answers that can break a rule. And the exact output each one should give.
The AI lists five. 1 and 10 are boundary values, the points where the result changes. The last case is three wrong answers: three questions, then 1 tea.
She runs every case on the AI's code. Here is case 4: three questions, then 5. It passes.

visual.heading: Asha runs every case on the AI's code
visual.label: Test

segments.say: Cases 1 to 4 pass. 1 and 10 are accepted, and wrong answers are asked again.
But case 5 fails. Three wrong answers should end in too many tries. The program asks a fourth time.
Here is case 5. She types 0 three times. The program does not stop. It asks a fourth time.
She types 5, and it takes it. The limit never worked. With more zeros, it would ask forever.

visual.heading: Debug: a trace before a fix

messages.text: Case 5 failed: it asked a fourth time, and took my 5. First trace the loop for 0, 0, 0 in a table, one line per pass. Then tell me which value never changes, and the smallest fix.

Pass 1: `teas` 0, `tries` 1. True.
Pass 2: `teas` 0, `tries` 1. True.
Pass 3: `teas` 0, `tries` 1. True.
`tries` is 1 on every pass. No line inside the loop changes it, so `tries < 3` is always True. Fix: add `tries += 1` as the last line inside the loop.

segments.say: Stage 5: debug. Asha pastes the loop and the failed run. She asks for a trace table first, then the value that never changes, then the fix.
The trace shows it clearly. Tries is 1 on every pass. Nothing inside the loop changes it, so tries less than 3 is always True. The fix: tries plus equals 1, inside the loop.
Asha writes the trace as a table, like step 5. Three passes, and tries is 1 every time.
That matches her run: one first question, plus three passes, is four questions. The trace and the run agree.

visual.heading: The fix: tries changes on every pass

segments.say: Here is the fix on line 7. Now tries goes 1, 2, 3, and the third wrong answer ends the loop.
Too many tries, using 1 tea. Exactly what the AI promised in the first place.

visual.heading: All cases again, on the fixed code
visual.label: Test

segments.say: A fix can break something else. So Asha runs every case again, on the fixed code.
All five pass. Now she trusts it.

messages.text: Suggest at most two readability improvements, each with one reason. Do not change how many times it asks.

1. Add a comment above the loop: `# Ask at most 3 times`.
2. Change `tries < 3` to `tries <= 3`, so the customer gets three full tries.
Suggestion 2 changes a condition. Before I accept it, I will count the questions it asks.

segments.say: Stage 6: improve. Asha asks for at most two readability improvements that do not change how many times it asks.
Suggestion 1, a comment, helps a reader. Suggestion 2 says: change less than 3 to less than or equal to 3, for three full tries.
Asha does not accept it yet. She will count the questions.

visual.heading: Testing suggestion 2
visual.hidden_text: Count the questions before the output appears.
visual.note: The user will type: 0 every time

segments.say: Here is the suggested condition on line 4: tries less than or equal to 3. Trace it in your head. Tries is 1, then 2, then 3.

ask.question: With `tries <= 3`, how many times does it ask before `Too many tries`?

after.say: Four times. When tries is 3, the condition is still True, so there is one more pass.
And Asha had said: do not change how many times it asks. The AI ignored that. She keeps less than 3, and adds only the comment.

visual.question: A loop never ends. What do you ask the AI for first?
options: A trace table of each pass
visual.explain: A trace shows which value never changes, before any fix.

segments.say: Quick check. A loop never ends. What do you ask the AI for first?

after.say: B. A trace table of each pass. It shows which value never changes.

items: Plan, write, generate, test, debug, improve.
Every value in the condition needs a line that changes it.
Count the questions: `<` and `<=` differ by one pass.

segments.say: Breather. Asha caught two AI mistakes, with a trace, and by counting.
Next, the four mistakes beginners make most with loops. You have already seen one of them.

scenes.title: Common mistakes
scenes.direction: Mistake 1 is a real error. Mistake 2 is a spot-it question about the counter. Mistake 3 shows the never-ending loop as a fragment and how to stop it. Mistake 4 is a spot-it on capital letters.

visual.heading: Mistake 1: a name with no value yet

segments.say: Mistake 1. The condition on line 2 is checked before the first pass. But answer does not exist yet.
Python stops with a Name Error. The fix: ask once before the loop, as in step 2, or use while True with break, as in step 4.

visual.heading: Mistake 2: your turn to spot it
visual.hidden_text: Find the mistake before the output appears.

segments.say: Now you try. Asha wants to serve tables 1 to 3. Compare line 3 with step 1.

ask.question: Asha wants tables 1 to 3. Which table is never served, and why?

after.say: Table 3. Less than 3 is False when table is 3, so the loop stops one pass too early.
after.heading: Mistake 2: one pass too few

after.say: No error, only a missing table. This is called an off-by-one error. The fix: less than or equal to 3.

visual.heading: Mistake 3: a loop that never ends
visual.label: Common mistakes
body: Illustrative only: do not run it as it is. To stop a running program, click in the terminal and press **Ctrl+C**.
visual.pre:
# illustrative: the counter never changes
table = 1
while table <= 3:
    print(f"Serving table {table}")

# prints "Serving table 1" again and again
# Ctrl+C stops it: KeyboardInterrupt

segments.say: Mistake 3 is the one the AI made. Nothing inside this loop changes table, so it prints table 1 again and again, forever.
If a program never stops, click in the terminal and press Control and C together. Python stops with a Keyboard Interrupt message.
The fix: add the line that changes the counter, inside the loop.

visual.heading: Mistake 4: spot this one too
visual.hidden_text: Find the reason before the output appears.
visual.note: The user will type: tea, Done, then done

segments.say: One more. The loop stops on done, in small letters. The user types Done, with a capital D.

ask.question: The user types `Done` with a capital D. What happens?

after.say: Done is added to the order as if it were an item. The loop keeps going until done in small letters.
after.heading: Mistake 4: capital letters in a stop value

after.say: The fix is the one from step 4: compare the answer after strip and lower.

items: Give every name a value before the loop.
Check the last pass: `<` or `<=`?
Ctrl+C stops a loop that never ends.

segments.say: Last breather. Now you know the four most common loop mistakes.
Two questions to think about on your own come next.

visual.heading: Recap
visual.label: What you learned
items: A `while` loop repeats its block while the condition is `True`.
A line inside the loop must change the value the condition checks.
A counter counts passes; a running total grows. `+=` and `-=` are short forms.
A stop value or `break` ends the loop when the user is finished.
A trace table shows every value on every pass.
Ask AI to trace a loop, then run the same answers yourself.

segments.say: Let's recap.
A while loop repeats its block while the condition is True.
A line inside the loop must change the value that the condition checks.
A counter counts passes, and a running total grows. Plus equals and minus equals are short forms.
A stop value or break ends the loop. And a trace table shows every value on every pass.
And with AI: ask for a trace, then run the same answers yourself.

visual.question: `n = 10`, then `while n > 0:` with `print(n)` and `n -= 3` inside. How many numbers print?
visual.explain: 10, 7, 4 and 1 print. Then n is -2, and -2 > 0 is False.

segments.say: One last check. N starts at 10. While n is greater than 0, the loop prints n, then takes away 3. How many numbers print?

after.say: D. Four: 10, 7, 4 and 1. Then n is minus 2, and the loop ends.
